To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the PC12 cell aggregates grow in the rat brain, express tyrosine hydroxy- 2 1 lase (TH), and are immunoreactive for TH.
PC12 cell aggregates placed into the brain of adult rats survive, grow processes, and are vascularized by host-derived microvessals.
PC12 cells can be transplanted into rat brain, grow in the host brain, and produce catecholamine neurotransmitters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the morphological and immunocytochemical characteristics of PC12 cell graft in the rat brain.
the use of PC12 cells as a potential source of trophic factors for the repair of the injured brain.
the morphological and functional characteristics of PC12 cell aggregates implanted into different regions of the brain of SpragueDawley rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PC12 cell aggregates do not appear to have any adverse effect on the host brain.
there is no evidence that the PC12 cell aggregates have a trophic influence on the host brain, although the possibility that such effects may occur cannot be excluded.
PC12 cells, when transplanted into the brain, do not form an effective vascular barrier and are not protected from immune attack, as are embryonic brain cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PC12 cells, when placed into the rat brain, are not rejected, but rather become integrated with the host brain, forming a vascular barrier that is not impermeable to large molecules.
the PC12 cells in the grafts were not only viable, but were also able to grow processes in the brain of the recipient animals.

PC12 cell grafting in brain is a feasible and useful model for the study of the interaction between the graft and host brain, and that the PC12 cells can survive and grow in the brain, where they may serve as a biosynthetic prosthesis to supply catecholamines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain can be a very good environment for growing cells.
the PC12 cell aggregates, in the absence of a trophic stimulus, do not grow in the adult brain.
we have demonstrated that the PC12 cells are not a viable solution to the problem of the brain-brain-brain-brain.
